summary: Compares several NAT traversal techniques that were considered for RTP media flows controlled by RTSP. For each, it describes use, security implications and deployment issues.

plainLanguage.summary: Several ways to get a video stream through a home router, compared with pros and cons.

subtitle: Comparing techniques for RTP media streams through NATs when controlled by RTSP

tldr.problem: When a streaming media server sends video or audio over RTP to a client behind a NAT (home router), the NAT blocks the incoming media stream because the connection was initiated by the client, not the server. RTSP (Real-Time Streaming Protocol) signals the stream setup but cannot send media through the NAT without additional techniques.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC evaluates nine different NAT traversal techniques: STUN (address discovery), ICE (connectivity establishment), Latching (hole-punching), TCP tunneling, TURN (media relay), Application Level Gateways, and others. Each technique has trade-offs in complexity, security, and applicability to different NAT and firewall types.
tldr.outcome: The evaluation guided the selection of ICE as the NAT traversal mechanism for RTSP 2.0. The RFC remains a reference for understanding NAT traversal design choices and their security implications.

facts.label: Primary use case
facts.value: Server on public internet, client behind NAT

today: RFC 7604 was published in 2015 as an Informational RFC documenting evaluation work for RTSP 2.0. ICE was chosen as the NAT traversal mechanism for RTSP 2.0 because it offers robust connectivity discovery across all NAT types. The RFC remains relevant for understanding the design trade-offs in NAT traversal and for protocols with similar media-control properties. Some techniques mentioned (such as RTP No-Op) were not standardized and are no longer available.

sections.title: The NAT Traversal Problem
sections.content:
Network Address Translator (NAT) devices, commonly home routers, create a discontinuity between internal private IP addresses and external public addresses. RTSP (Real-Time Streaming Protocol) is a media control protocol that carries network address and port information in its messages, but the media itself flows over RTP (Real-Time Transport Protocol) using UDP.

The problem is that when an RTSP client initiates a SETUP request from inside a NAT, the NAT creates a mapping for the RTSP control flow. However, when the server tries to send media back on a different UDP port, the NAT blocks it because no outgoing packet from that port has created a mapping. Additionally, firewalls often block traffic unless an application-level gateway understands the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Your router knows to let your streaming app's control messages through. But when the server tries to send the actual video, the router does not know who asked for it, so it blocks it.

sections.title: NAT Behavior and Firewall Types
sections.content:
The RFC reviews NAT behavioral requirements from RFC 4787. Key behaviors include how a NAT reuses port mappings (endpoint-independent, address-dependent, or address/port-dependent) and how it filters incoming traffic. Different NAT devices exhibit different behaviors, and a traversal technique must work across all types.

Firewalls are discussed as a separate concern. While firewalls and NATs serve different purposes (firewalls enforce security policy, NATs translate addresses), many SOHO devices combine both. The RFC notes that some NAT traversal solutions also solve firewall traversal, but a specialized Application Level Gateway (ALG) may provide better control for firewalls alone.
sections.plainLanguage: Different routers handle translations differently. Some remember where packets came from, others just remember the addresses. This matters for choosing the right trick.

sections.title: Nine NAT Traversal Techniques
sections.content:
Stand-Alone STUN has the client ask a STUN server to report the client's external IP and port, then the client tells the RTSP server to send to those addresses. This works only if the NAT gives the same external address to all peers.

ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) is more robust: the client and server each collect multiple possible addresses (host addresses, STUN-discovered addresses, relay addresses) and try them in parallel until a working path is found. ICE includes STUN servers running on the media ports themselves, so the server can verify connectivity before sending media.

Latching exploits NAT symmetry: the client sends a packet to the server's media port first (a hole-punching packet), and the server replies to the source address of that packet. This works for all NAT types but requires the server to be outside the NAT and is vulnerable to spoofing attacks unless the server restricts by source address.

TURN (Traversal Using Relays) has a relay server forward all media. This always works but adds latency and requires a relay infrastructure. TCP Tunneling sends media over TCP through the NAT-friendly RTSP connection instead of UDP.

Application Level Gateways are ALGs embedded in the NAT or firewall that understand RTSP and automatically open pinholes. Three-Way Latching and other variations add authentication to prevent spoofing.
sections.plainLanguage: STUN asks a helper what your address looks like. ICE tries multiple paths. Latching makes you knock first. TURN uses a relay. Some routers that understand RTSP handle it automatically.

sections.title: Trade-Offs: Complexity, Security, and Applicability
sections.content:
Each technique has different strengths. STUN is simple but fragile across NAT types. ICE is robust but has high implementation burden and setup delay. Latching has minimal delay but is vulnerable to DDoS attacks using forged source addresses. TURN is reliable but expensive and adds latency.

The RFC emphasizes that choosing a technique requires balancing several concerns. Implementation burden falls on server, client, or middlebox differently for each method. Some techniques require RTSP protocol extensions, others do not. Security considerations include DDoS attacks, where an attacker tricks the RTSP server into sending media to the attacker's target IP address, causing the server to amplify the attack.

The document notes that several techniques fall into the UNSAF (Unilateral Self-Address Fixing) category, which the IETF recommends only as temporary solutions pending IPv6 deployment or NAT elimination.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tricks are simple but do not always work. Others work everywhere but are slow or complicated. Some can be abused to attack other computers. Picking one is about balancing speed, cost, and reliability.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios and Firewall Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC discusses how different use cases drive different choices. For a streaming server on the public internet (the main use case), simple solutions like stand-alone STUN may suffice. For a server behind a NAT (a lower-priority use case), ICE or TURN is needed.

Firewalls add complexity: a firewall ALG that understands RTSP can automatically open pinholes, but if the ALG does not support a given traversal method, it may interfere. Using TLS to encrypt RTSP messages prevents ALGs from reading them, which solves ALG interference but breaks firewall-based policy enforcement.

The document lists requirements for any solution: it must work for all NAT types, should minimize impact on clients not behind NATs, must be simple to use and administer, and must defend against DDoS attacks by authenticating that the client actually wants to receive media at the claimed address.
sections.plainLanguage: If the server is on the internet, you can use a simple trick. If it is behind the router, you need a stronger one. Your router may understand RTSP and help, or it may get confused and break things.
